title: Lesson 30: Capstone: Run Your Own Engagement End to End
description: Run a full engagement from discovery through handover: the complete arc, the seams between phases, and how each prior lesson connects so you can carry an engagement to a clean close without a safety net.

questions.question: Where do engagements most often break down?
options: In the middle of a single phase when one technique is weak
At the seams, where one phase is not finished in a way that feeds the next
Whenever the client refuses to sign a contract
Because the tool cannot handle the client's data volume
questions.explanation: An engagement usually fails not because one phase was done badly but because a phase was not completed in a way that connected to the next, so watching the seams catches most trouble.

questions.question: What is the fix for a scope that lists inclusions but excludes nothing?
options: Adding inclusions until the client stops asking for more
Writing exclusions plainly, since they stop scope creep
Lowering the price so new requests feel expensive
Waiting for the client to withdraw their requests
questions.explanation: A scope with only inclusions cannot stop scope creep, because every new request appears to be part of the problem; written exclusions are what keep the work on time and on budget.

questions.question: When should an agent's guardrails be set during an engagement?
options: Added after the agent is built, as a cleanup step
Left out, since they unnecessarily limit the agent
Applied only to irreversible actions, later in the build
Set during scoping and built in from the start
questions.explanation: Guardrails are part of the design, decided during scoping and implemented as part of the build; adding them afterward means retrofitting safety onto a system that was built without limits.
